The Oyo State Government has vowed to resist any attempt by the National Union of Road Transport Workers to take over public motor parks in the state, insisting that a recent Court of Appeal judgment did not grant the union such rights. The government said any attempt to forcibly seize, occupy or interfere with the management of public motor parks would be resisted through all lawful means. The position followed a seven-day ultimatum issued by the NURTW, threatening to reclaim motor parks across the state’s 33 local government areas over the alleged disobedience of court judgments recognising its right to manage the facilities. In a statement issued on Monday in Ibadan, the state capital, the Special Adviser to the Governor on Media, Sulaimon Olarenwaju, said the government remained committed to obeying lawful judicial decisions but rejected what it described as a misrepresentation of the Court of Appeal’s judgment. Olarenwaju maintained that the judgment only reaffirmed citizens’ constitutional right to freedom of association and did not direct the government to hand over public motor parks to the union. He said, “The judgment merely reaffirmed the constitutional right of citizens to freedom of association. It did not confer ownership, control, or management of public assets on any union, nor did it authorise any organisation to take over facilities built, maintained, and regulated by government. “Accordingly, any attempt to rely on the judgment as a basis for demanding, threatening, or effecting the takeover of public motor parks is a clear misinterpretation of the court’s decision and has no basis in law.” The government described public motor parks as assets owned by local government councils and could not be claimed or administered by any union on the strength of the right to freedom of association. It added that while members of the NURTW and other transport unions were free to associate and organise in accordance with the law, such rights did not extend to the forceful occupation or control of public facilities. According to the government, alternative arrangements were introduced to restore order in the transport sector, protect lives and property, and ensure peaceful operations at motor parks. It said the relative peace and stability recorded in the sector in recent years demonstrated the effectiveness of the arrangements, adding that it would not allow a return to an era characterised by violence, thuggery and insecurity. The government urged the NURTW leadership and members to study the Court of Appeal judgment carefully and pursue their interests through lawful channels rather than actions capable of creating tension or threatening public peace. It further cautioned the union against using the judgment to justify what it described as an unlawful assumption of authority over public assets. “For the avoidance of doubt, while members of the NURTW remain free to associate, hold meetings, conduct lawful activities, and pursue their interests through legitimate channels, they do not possess any court-backed right to seize, control, or administer motor parks owned by the government or local government councils,” the statement added. SERAP appeals N100m defamation award, awaits A’Court ruling Oyo APM gov candidate pledges to sustain Makinde’s LAUTECH projects 2027: Court of Appeal warns elections tribunal staff against bribery The government insisted that it would continue to protect public assets, preserve order and safeguard residents, warning that no individual or organisation would be allowed to disrupt existing arrangements through threats or intimidation. The NURTW, however, dared the governor, insisting there was no going back on its plan to resume full operations in all motor parks across the state on Monday, November 23. The union, in a statement jointly signed by its chairman, Abideen Olajide, popularly known as Ejiogbe and secretary, Lekan Alesinloye, in Ibadan, the state capital, dismissed the government’s reaction to its seven-day ultimatum as a spurious misrepresentation of a binding Court of Appeal judgment. The union said its confidence rested on the unanimous judgment of the Court of Appeal, Ibadan Division, delivered on September 26, 2025, in Appeal No: CA/IB/263/2022, where Justice Kenneth Amadi held that the government “failed to justify the suspension” and “set aside the suspension on the operations of the Appellant in Oyo State. It added, “To set aside a suspension is to restore what was suspended. Even a first-year law student knows that. Only a government determined to disobey the law will pretend not to understand it.” The union said the government’s position was further destroyed by its admission before the court. In a Notice of Preliminary Objection dated April 23, 2026, filed by the Attorney-General, Mr Abiodun Aikomo, the government stated that “the 2nd respondent has not done anything whatsoever to prevent the NURTW, the appellant herein, from its operations in Oyo State. “A government cannot confess in court that it is not stopping us and then turn around in a press release to say we cannot operate. That is not rule of law. That is double-speak.” The union argued that it was not a street gang or a creation of any governor, but a creation of law; statutorily established under Decree 4 of 1996, now the Trade Unions Act, and protected by the 1999 Constitution (as amended) under Section 40 on freedom of association, Section 1(1) and (3) on constitutional supremacy, and Section 287(2), which commands that decisions of the Court of Appeal “shall be enforced in any part of the Federation by all authorities and persons.” It punctured the government’s claim that parks are public assets owned by local government councils, insisting that the government owned only four terminals in Ibadan and nothing more throughout the state, while all the transport motors plying the roads belong to the NURTW for control. “The government does not own a single tyre, a single engine, a single steering wheel on those roads. A government that owns only four terminals cannot use them as a licence to proscribe a national union for seven and a half years,” the statement said. The union said its members had endured seven and a half years of hunger, humiliation and deaths after the proscription, while previous judgments in its favour were ignored, adding, “Our members are not criminals. They are fathers, mothers and breadwinners who have been denied dignity for too long. An injustice to one is an injustice to all. Enough is enough.” It said it had alerted the Federal Government, the General Officer Commanding, the Director of DSS, the Commissioner of Police and the NLC. The union demanded that the Attorney-General withdraw his interpretation, advise government and all park managers to vacate the parks, and publicly affirm the binding nature of the judgment, while calling on the Commissioner of Police to provide security and arrest anyone who obstructs its activities.
